newsitem.title: GERMANY: German minister wants new two-year Bosnia mandate.
newsitem.headline: German minister wants new two-year Bosnia mandate.

text.p: German Defence Minister Volker Ruehe said on Monday that a new international peacekeeping mandate for Bosnia must last no more than two years, but should initially be approved for one.

Ruehe has already pledged Bonn's support for a new mission if the United Nations and NATO, as seems likely, decide peacekeepers are needed to stay on in Bosnia after the mandate of the current force expires at the end of this year.
But until now he has spoken only of a one-year mandate.
"I believe one year makes sense but some people want a longer period, until the autumn of 1998, when the next elections take place in Bosnia," Ruehe told a news briefing.

The German parliament should initially give a green light for a new German deployment of one year, "and then we can see what happens," Ruehe said. "The thinking is for one year or two, but anything more than that is unimaginable."

Ruehe repeated that Germany, gradually shedding its post-war reluctance to send troops abroad, would expect to play a full military role in a renewed peacekeeping mission, going beyond the engineering and logistics role it plays in the IFOR contingent.
Germany expects to cooperate with France in the sector of Bosnia where Paris leads the peacekeeping operation, and possibly send part of a joint Franco-German brigade to join the next mission.

Ruehe said he did not expect NATO defence ministers meeting in the Norwegian town of Bergen on Wednesday and Thursday to determine the likely shape of a new post-IFOR force, but that they would take stock of the political situation in Bosnia.

The United States has yet to commit itself to a new peacekeeping mandate and is unlikely to do so before the presidential election in November. But Ruehe said any new mission must also include U.S. ground forces.
The minister said he hoped a new peacekeeping force would have a brief to detain Bosnian leaders charged with war crimes.
"In the long term it damages the credibility of the peace process if NATO-led peacekeepers are operating alongside people who have perpetrated war crimes," he said.
In Bergen, the ministers are also likely to discuss efforts to agree an institutional framework linking NATO and Russia before NATO admits new members from eastern Europe.
Ruehe said Germany was spearheading these discussions for NATO alongside the United States, and that he was confident of an agreement before a NATO summit in the first half of 1997.
"We have gone beyond polemics," he said. "Our negotiations are concrete and matter-of-fact."
The informal Bergen meeting will also examine plans for a streamlining of internal NATO command structures.

Ruehe said there was still no agreement between the United States and the European allies on who should command NATO forces in a new European southern region, including the U.S. 6th fleet in the Mediterranean.
The German minister said the increased commitment of France and Spain to NATO's military structures made it all the more important that Europe should command the southern flank.
He said a possible solution could be to subordinate the 6th fleet directly to NATO's Supreme Allied Commander Europe, an American.
